summary: The card types are artifact, battle, conspiracy, creature, dungeon, enchantment, instant, kindred, land, phenomenon, plane, planeswalker, scheme, sorcery, and vanguard.
Some objects have more than one card type (for example, an artifact creature).
An object that’s both a land and another card type (for example, an artifact land) can only be played as a land.
Each kindred card has another card type.
A player who has priority may cast an artifact card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
When an artifact spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
Artifact subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: “Artifact — Equipment.” Artifact subtypes are also called artifact types.
Artifacts have no characteristics specific to their card type.
Some artifacts have the subtype “Equipment.” An Equipment can be attached to a creature.
The creature an Equipment is attached to is called the “equipped creature.” The Equipment is attached to, or “equips,” that creature.
Equipment spells are cast like other artifact spells.
An Equipment that’s also a creature can’t equip a creature unless that Equipment has reconfigure (see rule 702.151, “Reconfigure”).
An Equipment’s controller is separate from the equipped creature’s controller; the two need not be the same.

If an effect attempts to put an Equipment that isn’t also an Aura (see rule 303.4i) onto the battlefield attached to either an object it can’t legally equip or an object that is undefined, the Equipment enters the battlefield unattached.
An ability of a permanent that refers to the “equipped creature” refers to whatever creature that permanent is attached to, even if the permanent with the ability isn’t an Equipment.
Some artifacts have the subtype “Fortification.” A Fortification can be attached to a land.
Some artifacts have the subtype “Vehicle.” Most Vehicles have a crew ability which allows them to become artifact creatures.
Each Vehicle has a printed power and toughness, but it has these characteristics only if it’s also a creature.
If a Vehicle becomes a creature, it immediately has its printed power and toughness.
A player who has priority may cast a creature card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
When a creature spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
Creature subtypes are usually a single word long and are listed after a long dash: “Creature — Human Soldier,” “Artifact Creature — Golem,” and so on.
Power and toughness are characteristics only creatures have.
A creature’s power is the amount of damage it deals in combat.
A creature’s toughness is the amount of damage needed to destroy it.
To determine a creature’s power and toughness, start with the numbers printed in its lower right corner, then apply any applicable continuous effects.
Creatures can attack and block.

A creature’s activated ability with the tap symbol or the untap symbol in its activation cost can’t be activated unless the creature has been under its controller’s control continuously since their most recent turn began.
Damage dealt to a creature by a source with neither wither nor infect is marked on that creature (see rule 120.3).
A player who has priority may cast an enchantment card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
When an enchantment spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
Enchantment subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: “Enchantment — Shrine.” Each word after the dash is a separate subtype.
Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player.
An Aura spell requires a target, which is defined by its enchant ability.
The object or player an Aura is attached to is called enchanted.

If an Aura is enchanting an illegal object or player as defined by its enchant ability and other applicable effects, the object it was attached to no longer exists, or the player it was attached to has left the game, the Aura is put into its owner’s graveyard.
An Aura can’t enchant itself.
An Aura’s controller is separate from the enchanted object’s controller or the enchanted player; the two need not be the same.

If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefiel
If an Aura is entering the battlefield and there is no legal object or player for it to enchant, the Aura remains in its current zone, unless that zone is the stack.
If an effect attempts to put a permanent that isn’t an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification onto the battlefield attached to an object or player, it enters the battlefield unattached.

If an effect attempts to put an Aura onto the battlefield attached to either an object or player it can’t legally enchant or an object or player that is undefined, the Aura remains in its current zone, unless that zone is the stack.
If an effect attempts to attach an Aura on the battlefield to an object or player it can’t legally enchant, the Aura doesn’t move.

If an effect allows an Aura that’s being turned face up to become attached to an object or player, the Aura’s controller considers the characteristics of that Aura as it would exist if it were face up to determine what it may be attached to, and they must choose a legal object or player according to
An ability of a permanent that refers to the “enchanted [object or player]” refers to whatever object or player that permanent is attached to, even if the permanent with the ability isn’t an Aura.
Some enchantments have the subtype “Saga.” See rule 714 for more information about Saga cards.
Some enchantments have the subtype “Class.” See rule 716 for more information about Class cards.
Some Aura enchantments also have the subtype “Role.”
If a permanent has more than one Role controlled by the same player attached to it, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its owner’s graveyard.
A player who has priority may cast an instant card from their hand.
When an instant spell resolves, the actions stated in its rules text are followed.
Instant subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: “Instant — Arcane.” Each word after the dash is a separate subtype.
Instants can’t enter the battlefield.
If text states that a player may do something “any time they could cast an instant” or “only as an instant,” it means only that the player must have priority.
A player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
A player can normally play one land during their turn; however, continuous effects may increase this number.

To determine whether a player can play a land, compare the number of lands the player can play this turn with the number of lands they have already played this turn (including lands played as special actions and lands played during the resolution of spells and abilities).
A player can’t play a land, for any reason, if the number of lands the player can play this turn is equal to or less than the number of lands they have already played this turn.
A player can’t play a land, for any reason, if it isn’t their turn.
Effects may also allow players to “put” lands onto the battlefield.
Land subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash.
The basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.
If an effect sets a land’s subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type.
Any land with the supertype “basic” is a basic land.
If an object is both a land and another card type, it can be played only as a land.
A player who has priority may cast a planeswalker card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
When a planeswalker spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
Planeswalker subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: “Planeswalker — Jace.” Each word after the dash is a separate subtype.
Previously, planeswalkers were subject to a “planeswalker uniqueness rule” that stopped a player from controlling two planeswalkers of the same planeswalker type.
Loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have.
The loyalty of a planeswalker card not on the battlefield is equal to the number printed in its lower right corner.

A planeswalker has the intrinsic ability “This permanent enters with a number of loyalty counters on it equal to its printed loyalty number.” This ability creates a replacement effect (see rule 614.1c).
The loyalty of a planeswalker on the battlefield is equal to the number of loyalty counters on it.
Each planeswalker has a number of loyalty abilities, which are activated abilities with loyalty symbols in their costs.
Planeswalkers can be attacked.

Previously, planeswalkers were subject to a redirection effect that allowed a player to have noncombat damage that would be dealt to an opponent be dealt to a planeswalker under that opponent’s control instead.
Damage dealt to a planeswalker results in that many loyalty counters being removed from it.
If a planeswalker’s loyalty is 0, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard.
A player who has priority may cast a sorcery card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
When a sorcery spell resolves, the actions stated in its rules text are followed.
Sorcery subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: “Sorcery — Arcane.” Each word after the dash is a separate subtype.
Sorceries can’t enter the battlefield.

If a spell, ability, or effect states that a player can do something only “any time they could cast a sorcery” or “only as a sorcery,” it means only that the player must have priority, it must be during the main phase of their turn, and the stack must be empty.

Similarly, if an effect checks to see if a spell was cast “any time a sorcery couldn’t have been cast,” it’s checking only whether the spell’s controller cast it without having priority, during a phase other than their main phase, or while another object was on the stack.
Each kindred card has another card type.

Kindred subtypes are usually a single word long and are listed after a long dash: “Kindred Enchantment — Merfolk.” The set of kindred subtypes is the same as the set of creature subtypes; these subtypes are called creature types.
Some older kindred cards were printed with the “tribal” card type.
Dungeon is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards.
Dungeon cards begin outside the game.
If a player ventures into the dungeon while they don’t own a dungeon card in the command zone, they choose a dungeon card they own from outside the game and put it into the command zone.
A dungeon card that’s brought into the game is put into the command zone until it leaves the game.
Dungeon cards are not permanents.
If an effect other than a venture into the dungeon keyword action would bring a dungeon card into the game from outside the game, it doesn’t; that card remains outside the game.
A player can own only one dungeon card in the command zone at a time, and they can’t bring a dungeon card into the game if a dungeon card they own is in the command zone.
Each dungeon card has a series of rooms connected to one another with arrows.
As a player puts a dungeon they own into the command zone, they put their venture marker on the topmost room.
Each room has a name.
Each room has a triggered ability called a room ability whose effect is printed on the card.
The venture into the dungeon keyword action allows players to move their venture marker down the rooms of a dungeon card.

If a player ventures into the dungeon while they own a dungeon card in the command zone and their venture marker isn’t on that dungeon’s bottommost room, they move their venture marker from the room it is on to the next room, following the direction of an arrow pointing away from the room their vent

If a player ventures into the dungeon while they own a dungeon card in the command zone and their venture marker is on that dungeon card’s bottommost room, they remove that dungeon card from the game.

If a player’s venture marker is on the bottommost room of a dungeon card, and that dungeon card isn’t the source of a room ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, the dungeon card’s owner removes it from the game.
A player completes a dungeon as that dungeon card is removed from the game.
A player who has priority may cast a battle card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty.
When a battle spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
Battle subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: “Battle — Siege.” Battle subtypes are also called battle types.
Defense is a characteristic that battles have.
The defense of a battle card not on the battlefield is equal to the number printed in its lower right corner.
A battle has the intrinsic ability “This permanent enters with a number of defense counters on it equal to its printed defense number.” This ability creates a replacement effect (see rule 614.1c).
The defense of a battle on the battlefield is equal to the number of defense counters on it.
Battles can be attacked.
Damage dealt to a battle results in that many defense counters being removed from it.
If a Siege battle’s defense is 0 and it isn’t the source of an ability which has triggered but not yet left the stack, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard.
If a non-Siege battle’s defense is 0, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard.
Each battle has a player designated as its protector.
As a battle enters the battlefield, its controller chooses a player to be its protector.
A battle’s protector can never attack it.
A battle’s protector may block creatures attacking that battle with creatures they control.

If a battle’s protector is a different player than its controller, all rules and effects that refer to the “defending player” relative to a battle that is being attacked refer to that battle’s protector rather than its controller.
If a rule or effect refers to the player who protects a battle, it means the player who is that battle’s protector.
A battle can have only one protector at a time.
A battle’s protector doesn’t change if it stops being a battle or it becomes a copy of another battle.
A battle can’t be attached to players or permanents, even if it is also an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification.

If a battle that isn’t being attacked has no player designated as its protector, or its protector is a player who can’t be its protector, its controller chooses an appropriate player to be its protector.
Some battles have the subtype Siege.
As a Siege enters the battlefield, its controller must choose its protector from among their opponents.
Sieges have the intrinsic ability “When the last defense counter is removed from this permanent, exile it, then you may cast it transformed without paying its mana cost.”
Plane is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards.
Plane cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, both while they’re part of a planar deck and while they’re face up.
Plane subtypes are listed after a long dash, and may be multiple words: “Plane — Serra’s Realm.” All words after the dash are, collectively, a single subtype.
A plane card may have any number of static, triggered, and/or activated abilities.
The controller of a face-up plane card is the player designated as the planar controller.
A face-up plane card that’s turned face down becomes a new object.
Each plane card has a triggered ability that triggers “Whenever chaos ensues.” These are called chaos abilities.
Phenomenon is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards.
Phenomenon cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, both while they’re part of a planar deck and while they’re face up.
Phenomenon cards have no subtypes.
The controller of a face-up phenomenon card is the player designated as the planar controller.
Each phenomenon card has a triggered ability that triggers when you encounter it.
A face-up phenomenon card that’s turned face down becomes a new object.

If a phenomenon card is face up in the command zone, and it isn’t the source of a triggered ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, the planar controller planeswalks the next time a player would receive priority.
Vanguard is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards.
Vanguard cards remain in the command zone throughout the game.
Vanguard cards have no subtypes.
A vanguard card may have any number of static, triggered, and/or activated abilities.
The owner of a vanguard card is the player who started the game with it in the command zone.
Each vanguard card has a hand modifier printed in its lower left corner.
Each vanguard card has a life modifier printed in its lower right corner.
Scheme is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards.
Scheme cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, both while they’re part of a scheme deck and while they’re face up.
Scheme cards have no subtypes.
A scheme card may have any number of static, triggered, and/or activated abilities.
The owner of a scheme card is the player who started the game with it in the command zone.

If a non-ongoing scheme card is face up in the command zone, and no triggered abilities of any scheme are on the stack or waiting to be put on the stack, that scheme card is turned face down and put on the bottom of its owner’s scheme deck the next time a player would receive priority.
If an ability of a scheme card includes the text “this scheme,” it means the scheme card in the command zone that’s the source of that ability.
Conspiracy cards are used only in limited play, particularly in the Conspiracy Draft variant (see rule 905).
At the start of a game, before decks are shuffled, each player may put any number of conspiracy cards from their sideboard into the command zone.
Conspiracy cards remain in the command zone throughout the game.
Conspiracy cards have no subtypes.
Conspiracy cards may have any number of static or triggered abilities.
Abilities of conspiracy cards may affect the start-of-game procedure.
Face-down conspiracy cards have no characteristics.
The owner of a conspiracy card is the player who put it into the command zone at the start of the game.
At any time, you may look at a face-down conspiracy card you control.
